q: How does the FOM define "operational control" with respect to a flight?
a: The exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight.

src.quote: Operational control with respect to a flight means the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight.
src.note: This is the core definition, repeated verbatim in 2.2.1. Remember the three verbs: initiating, conducting, terminating.

q: Who has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights?
a: The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO).

src.quote: The 14 CFR Part 119 designated Director of Operations (DO) has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights.
src.note: The DO sits at the top of the operational-control structure under Part 119.

q: To whom has the DO delegated the authority to conduct certain operational-control functions?
a: The Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO).

src.quote: The DO has delegated the authority to conduct certain functions to the Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO).
src.note: The FODO acts on delegated DO authority for daily oversight of line flying operations.

q: For what three items are the PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher jointly responsible under Joint Responsibility?
a: The preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight.

src.quote: The PIC and Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight in compliance with Federal Aviation Regulations
src.note: Both must agree the flight can be accomplished safely; agreement is shown by their signatures on the Dispatch Release.

q: If the flight cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions but the PIC believes there is no safer procedure than continuing toward the airport, what does that continuation become?
a: An emergency.

src.quote: unless, in the opinion of the PIC, there is no safer procedure. In that event, continuation toward that airport is an emergency.
src.note: The PIC may not otherwise allow a flight to continue toward a dispatched airport if it cannot be completed safely due to hazardous conditions.

q: How is the PIC's and Dispatcher's agreement that the flight can be accomplished safely indicated?
a: By the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: Agreement is indicated by the signatures of the PIC and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release.
src.note: Both must agree the flight as planned can be accomplished safely and in accordance with 14 CFR and Company policy.

q: When conditions change enroute so the flight cannot be conducted in accordance with the Dispatch Release, who is required to contact whom?
a: The person encountering or learning of the changed conditions must contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: it is required that the person encountering or learning of the changed conditions contact the other to institute the necessary amendment to the Dispatch Release.
src.note: The duty to initiate an amendment falls on whoever learns of the change first, PIC or Dispatcher.

q: What is the scope of the PIC's control and authority over other crewmembers during flight time?
a: Full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing those duties.

src.quote: The PIC has full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time, whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing them to perform the duties of those crewmembers.
src.note: This mirrors 14 CFR 91.3 PIC authority; crewmembers shall comply with the PIC's orders.

q: What must happen if the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations?
a: The operation will be stopped.

src.quote: If the PIC is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations, then the operation will be stopped.
src.note: When in doubt about safety or compliance, the default is to stop, not to press on.

q: During a training or evaluation event conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, who is the designated PIC?
a: The Check Pilot is the designated PIC.

src.quote: Any time a training/evaluation event is being conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, the Check Pilot is the designated PIC.
src.note: This shifts designated PIC status to the Check Pilot whenever they run the event from a pilot seat.

q: For what period is the PIC's control and authority in effect (Duration of Command)?
a: From the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight.

src.quote: The PIC's control and authority is in effect from the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight.
src.note: Command authority begins at report-for-duty, not at pushback, and runs through flight termination.

q: What is the sequence of command listed in the Chain of Command?
a: Captain (PIC); International Relief Officer (IRO)/Second in Command (SIC); PIC-qualified First Officer; First Officer; "A" Flight Attendant/FFA; Flight Attendants in descending order.

src.quote: The sequence of command is as follows:
src.note: The list runs Captain, IRO/SIC, PIC-qualified FO, FO, then the A Flight Attendant/FFA and remaining Flight Attendants.

q: On a flight with an augmented Flight Crew, who becomes the acting Captain when the assigned Captain begins their rest period?
a: The IRO becomes the acting Captain.

src.quote: when the assigned Captain begins their rest period, the IRO will become the acting Captain.
src.note: The IRO steps up to acting Captain for the duration of the Captain's rest on an augmented crew.

q: In the Flight Operations Structure, what role does the FODO serve relative to the Director of Operations?
a: The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations.

src.quote: The FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations.
src.note: Operational-control decisions are made under the DO's authority by the Dispatcher, the PIC, and, when required, the FODO.

q: When does the Operational Control Window (OCW) start and end for a normal flight?
a: It starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport.

src.quote: OCW starts two and a half hours (D-150) prior to the scheduled departure time and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport.
src.note: D-150 means 150 minutes (two and a half hours) before scheduled departure; the window closes at block-in.

q: For flights to South Korea, when does the Operational Control Window (OCW) start?
a: Three hours prior to scheduled departure (D-180), rather than the standard two and a half hours (D-150).

src.quote: the OCW starts three hours (D-180).
src.note: South Korea flights get a longer, three-hour (D-180) window versus the standard D-150 (two and a half hours) — relevant to your 787 transpacific departures.

q: Within the OCW, a decision to cancel or modify a flight is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from whom, and who is ultimately responsible?
a: It requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible.

src.quote: any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC.
src.note: The FODO and Pilot Crew Scheduling provide guidance when required, but the DO is ultimately responsible.

q: May a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate act as PIC or IRO?
a: No. A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO.

src.quote: A Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO.
src.note: The IRO is SIC of the aircraft and assumes command if the Captain is incapacitated, so a restricted ATP is disqualifying for that seat.

q: What phases of flight constitute a Sterile Flight Deck (critical phases of flight)?
a: Ground operations involving pushback, towing, taxi, takeoff, and landing; and all other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight.

src.quote: All other flight operations conducted below 10,000 ft MSL, except cruise flight.
src.note: The deck is not considered sterile during lengthy ground holds when the parking brake is set.

q: What bank angle and nose-up pitch attitude should normal flying not require to be exceeded?
a: Bank angles greater than 30 degrees or pitch attitude greater than 20 degrees nose up.

src.ref: FOM 2.3.14 — Style of Flying/Bank and Pitch Angles
src.quote: Normal flying should not require bank angles greater than 30 or airspeeds higher than the normal limit speed or pitch attitude greater than 20 nose up.
src.note: Aircraft may exceed 20 nose up under certain flight conditions or departure/climb profiles.

q: Check-airman scenario: airborne, an event requires the PIC to deviate from a Company procedure and from an ATC clearance to keep the aircraft safe. What authority lets the PIC do this on their own?
a: The PIC may unilaterally exercise emergency authority.

src.quote: May unilaterally exercise emergency authority.
src.note: Listed among the PIC's responsibilities in the job description; echoes 14 CFR 91.3 emergency authority. "Unilaterally" means no prior coordination is required to act.

q: Check-airman scenario: enroute, the PIC is unsure whether a reroute still allows the flight to be conducted per the Dispatch Release. Per the FOM, who is the PIC's contact and the primary source of flight-status information?
a: The Dispatcher.

src.quote: When the PIC has an issue related to operational control of a flight, the PIC should contact the Dispatcher. The Dispatcher is the primary source of information related to the status of a flight
src.note: Under joint responsibility the Dispatcher — not crew scheduling or the gate — is the PIC's operational-control contact for delay, reroute, or cancellation.

q: Check-airman scenario: on an augmented crew, the Captain becomes incapacitated during cruise. Per the chain of command, who assumes command?
a: The IRO assumes command, performs the Captain's duties, and assumes the Captain's responsibilities.

src.quote: If the Captain becomes incapacitated, the IRO will assume command, perform the Captain's duties, and assume the Captain's responsibilities.
src.note: This is why a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ATP certificate must not act as PIC or IRO — the IRO can inherit command.

q: Check-airman scenario: inside the Operational Control Window, the NOC business group wants to cancel your flight for commercial reasons. What does the FOM require, and who is ultimately responsible?
a: Inside the OCW, canceling or modifying is an operational control action requiring coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC; the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible.

src.quote: Within the OCW, any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the PIC.
src.note: Contrast 2.2.2.2: before the OCW the same decision is a business decision that does not require operational-control endorsement.
